title: How AI Is Pushing India From Reactive to Preventive Healthcare
excerpt: From rural TB screening to AI chatbots bridging the doctor shortage, India is deploying artificial intelligence to overhaul a healthcare system that serves 1.4 billion people.
body:
• AI-driven diagnostics in India can detect conditions like tuberculosis and diabetic retinopathy at scale in areas with few specialists
  • India's diagnostics industry is projected to reach Rs 1,360 billion by FY2026, with AI driving a shift toward early detection and prevention
  • AI-powered fraud detection under PM-JAY has prevented fraudulent health insurance claims worth nearly Rs 630 crore
  • Experts warn that AI solutions trained on limited datasets may produce misleading results and call for rigorous testing frameworks

India's healthcare system — stretched thin by a shortage of specialists and a disease burden that spans tropical infections and chronic lifestyle conditions — is turning to artificial intelligence to make a fundamental shift from reactive treatment to preventive care.

Diagnostics at Scale

The most immediate impact is in AI-assisted diagnostics. AI-based X-ray analysis can flag tuberculosis cases, while smartphone-based eye screening detects cataracts and diabetic retinopathy at scale — conditions that are common but chronically underdiagnosed in rural India due to the lack of ophthalmologists, according to a NASSCOM-Kantar report on AI in Indian healthcare.

"AI improves workflows, enhances clinical capacity, and acts as a force multiplier," said a senior official from the National Health Authority in an interview with eGov. "Smartphone-based eye screening can detect cataracts at scale. This allows mass screening using the same workforce, which is critical for a country as large and diverse as India."

""A solution trained on limited or localized datasets may produce misleading results elsewhere."

AI is also being deployed to improve surveillance of vector-borne diseases like dengue and malaria, helping health authorities respond to outbreaks more efficiently. Research published in peer-reviewed journals has shown advanced machine learning models can detect Type 2 diabetes up to 28 months earlier than conventional diagnoses, achieving 89.6% accuracy.

Beyond the Clinic: Chatbots and Agentic AI

AI-driven chatbots and virtual assistants are helping patients navigate India's fragmented healthcare system, while humanoid robots like RIA — introduced at the Digital Health Summit — offer personalized health advice and interpret health data.

The India Development Review has explored whether AI chatbots can bridge India's healthcare gap, particularly in primary care settings where doctor availability remains a critical bottleneck. But the approach carries risks. A Nature Medicine study published in February 2026 found that OpenAI's ChatGPT Health tool — serving roughly 40 million daily users — under-triaged more than 50% of cases requiring immediate emergency care.

"A solution trained on limited or localized datasets may produce misleading results elsewhere. That is why we are developing an AI testing and benchmarking platform."

— National Health Authority official

Fraud Detection and Financial Impact

Beyond diagnostics, AI has proven its value in healthcare administration. AI-based anomaly detection in claims processing under PM-JAY, India's public health insurance scheme, has prevented fraudulent claims amounting to nearly Rs 630 crore, according to the National Health Authority. The technology creates accountability among hospitals while saving public funds.

India's diagnostics industry, projected to reach Rs 1,360 billion by FY2026, is increasingly driven by AI adoption across hospital information systems, electronic health records, and radiology information systems.

The Road Ahead

Experts emphasize that realizing AI's potential in Indian healthcare requires rigorous testing, infrastructure investment, and provider training. The NHA, in collaboration with IIT Kanpur, is developing an AI testing and benchmarking platform and organizing hackathons where solutions are validated against large, diverse datasets.

The transformation is still early. But for a country where the ratio of doctors to patients remains well below WHO recommendations, AI offers a path to extend the reach of existing healthcare capacity — provided the technology is deployed responsibly.
